newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran needs "fresh" foreign policy, says Khatami.
newsitem.headline: Iran needs "fresh" foreign policy, says Khatami.

text.p: Iran's President Mohammad Khatami told a parliament session debating his cabinet nominees on Tuesday that the Islamic republic needed an "active and fresh presence" in its foreign relations.

"In foreign relations we need an active and fresh presence based on our independence and national interests," he said. "It is important for us to defuse tensions and seek friendship and brotherhood in the international arena."
"We have to exploit all possibilities to promote and progress our country in the world based upon the three principles of dignity, wisdom and expediency," Khatami said.

Iran has no ties with the United States, which has imposed sanctions on the Islamic republic, and its relations with Europe are often tense. It has over the past year worked towards improving fragile ties with its Gulf Arab neighbours.
Analysts do not expect Khatami, sworn in on August 4, to make radical changes in foreign policy, the domain of supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Khatami was addressing the parliament, or Majlis, shortly after it opened to start debate on his proposed cabinet. It is expected to vote on the 22 cabinet nominees on Wednesday.
He asked parliament in his 50-minute address to give its vote of confidence to all ministers so "that the stagnation we are witnessing will come to an end as soon as possible".
The debate started after his address and the first three deputies who spoke supported all the nominees.
Khatami, a moderate 54-year-old Moslem Shi'ite cleric, is expected to lose at least one of his nominees at the hands of conservatives and radicals in parliament.
The final make-up of the cabinet is seen as crucial in setting the reforming tone of Khatami's four-year term.
Khatami told the 270-seat parliament his administration was based on the rule of law and increasing popular participation in politics and other areas of life.
"The two major principles of all plans and programmes are seeking the rule of law and attracting people's participation in political, social and cultural fields.

"As the elected president of the people I am here in the house of the people to present the names and the programmes of my colleagues whose success in serving the people depends on the representatives of the people," Khatami said.

"We have had many crises in the past years. Now it's the era of consolidating and stabilising the Islamic republic," he said. "This requires a powerful state but the basis of a powerful state is proper relations with the people so that the system should be based on law."

Khatami swept to power in elections in May after scooping the votes of Iranian youth, women and middle classes who saw in him a leader able to inject social and economic freedoms into the 18-year-old Islamic republic.

Despite the expected loss of at least one minister in a sensitive domestic portfolio, Khatami will still emerge with the majority of his cabinet largely intact and his election mandate for change undamaged, analysts said.

Opposition is expected from conservatives in parliament to Khatami's proposed minister of culture, Ataollah Mohajerani -- a controversial figure for his support in 1990 of a resumption of talks with Washington -- and interior minister Abdollah Nouri.

The Culture Ministry has emerged as a battleground between Khatami's supporters, who want to breathe more freedoms into the Islamic republic, and conservatives who see the ministry as the main weapon against "Western cultural invasion".
The ministry has power over what media, books, films and music are allowed in the country.

Khatami told parliament his main economic priorities were to eradicate poverty and increase people's purchasing power. He called for a greater involvement in the economy by the private sector and clarity in economic policies.
